subject: Banking
title: What Is Open Banking
description: A short lesson to help you apply What Is Open Banking.

hook.text: Open banking lets third-party apps access your bank data with your permission.

buildup.text: Traditionally, banks controlled all your data. If you wanted a loan, only your bank knew your history.

discovery.text: APIs now let fintech apps read your transactions, verify income, and initiate payments.

twist.text: The EU mandated open banking in 2018 with PSD2. Banks were forced to share data. They fought it but lost.

climax.text: Open banking shifts power from institutions to individuals.

punchline.text: Your data, your choice. Open banking breaks the bank's monopoly.

quiz.question: What does open banking allow?
options: Third-party apps to access your bank data with your permission via APIs

details.summary: Open banking is a regulatory framework that requires banks to share customer financial data with authorized third parties through secure APIs, when the customer consents, enabling new financial products built on bank-held information.
details.whyItMatters: Open banking breaks the monopoly banks have over customer data. By letting customers share their data with competitors and innovators, it drives competition, lowers fees, and enables a new generation of personalized financial services.
takeaways: Banks must share customer data via APIs when customers consent
The UK and EU led open banking regulation with PSD2
Open banking enables comparison tools, budgeting apps, and new lenders

faq.question: Does open banking compromise your privacy?
faq.answer: No, data is only shared with your explicit consent and can be revoked anytime. Third parties must be authorized and regulated. You control exactly what data is shared and with whom. Open banking actually gives you more control over your data.

faq.question: How has open banking changed banking in the UK?
faq.answer: Over 7 million UK consumers use open banking services. It has enabled new lending platforms, instant account-to-account payments, and budgeting tools. Traditional banks have been forced to improve products to compete with innovations.
